lesson.title: Building an Army from Scratch: The Draft Returns
lesson.summary: With only a small volunteer army in April 1917, Congress passed the Selective Service Act in May to conscript millions of men through local civilian draft boards, a system deliberately designed to avoid the violence and unfairness of the Civil War draft.
lesson.body:
When the United States declared war in April 1917, as described in the previous chapter, its regular army numbered only around two hundred thousand soldiers, a fraction of the millions already fighting and dying on the battlefields of Europe. Relying on volunteers alone was unlikely to raise an army fast enough or large enough to matter. Congress responded with the Selective Service Act, signed into law by Wilson on May 18, 1917.

The law required men to register for a possible draft, but it deliberately used a decentralized system of local civilian draft boards rather than a small number of federal officials making decisions from Washington. This design was no accident. It was meant to avoid a repeat of the deeply unpopular Civil War draft, in which wealthier men could pay for substitutes or buy exemptions outright, a system that had helped spark violent unrest, including the deadly New York City draft riots of 1863. By putting local community members in charge of decisions about deferments and exemptions, lawmakers hoped the process would feel fairer and more accountable.

Registration began on June 5, 1917, initially covering men between the ages of 21 and 30. As the war continued and the need for manpower grew, the age range was expanded in September 1918 to cover men from 18 to 45. In total, roughly 24 million men registered for the draft nationwide. About 2.8 million men were actually inducted into service through the draft, and when combined with volunteers and National Guard units, roughly 4 million Americans served in the U.S. military during the war, with about half eventually deployed overseas as part of the American Expeditionary Forces commanded by General John J. Pershing.

The draft was not universally welcomed. Some socialists and labor radicals argued the war served the interests of bankers and arms manufacturers rather than ordinary Americans, and a number of men resisted registration or induction outright, earning the era's dismissive label of slackers. As the next chapter shows, feeding, arming, and paying for this rapidly expanding military required mobilizing far more than just soldiers. It meant reorganizing much of American economic and social life around the war effort.
